chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The woman with istihaaza (inter-period bleeding) performs ghusl at the time of the Dhuhr prayer, then she prays Dhuhr and Asr. Then she performs ghusl at Maghrib, and prays Maghrib and Isha. Then she performs ghusl at the morning prayer and prays Fajr. And there is no problem for her husband to come to her whenever he wishes, except during the days of her menstruation (haydh), when her husband must abstain from her.
He said: And he (the Imam) said: No woman does this at all — seeking divine reward (ihtisab) — except that she would be cured of that condition.

key_terms.احْتِسَاباً: ihtisab — performing an act sincerely for the sake of divine reward, without worldly motive
key_terms.الْمُسْتَحَاضَةُ: istihaaza — the woman experiencing non-menstrual irregular vaginal bleeding, a specific fiqh category distinct from haydh (menstruation)
key_terms.حَيْض: haydh — menstruation; marital relations are strictly prohibited during this period unlike istihaaza

ai.seo_question: What are the ghusl rules for a woman with istihaaza (inter-period bleeding) in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (a.s.) lays out the rulings for a woman experiencing istihaaza (irregular/inter-period vaginal bleeding), specifying that she must perform three daily ghusl baths — before Dhuhr, Maghrib, and Fajr — and combine prayers accordingly. The ruling also affirms that marital relations remain permissible during istihaaza but are absolutely prohibited during actual menstruation (haydh). The Imam adds a spiritual dimension: any woman who faithfully observes these obligations seeking divine reward (ihtisab) will be cured of the condition, connecting ritual compliance with divine healing.
